title: Almost (Acts 26)
hook: King Agrippa says almost thou persuadest me

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul arrested in the Temple, telling his story from the barracks steps. Your line was tell what happened. Did anyone ask? Day five hundred fifty-six.

Two years pass. Paul sits in custody in Caesarea, on the coast, while governors come and go. Then a new governor, Festus, gets a royal visit: King Agrippa the Second and his sister Bernice arrive with great pomp, the text says, with commanders and the city's leading men. Festus has a prisoner he doesn't know what to do with, and the king is curious. So Paul is brought in, in chains, to a hall full of power. And he tells his story for the third time in Acts.
screen: `TWO YEARS IN CAESAREA.` → `A KING ARRIVES WITH GREAT POMP.` → `A PRISONER IN A HALL OF POWER.`

segments.voice: Paul tells it again: the road, the light at midday brighter than the sun, the voice. This time he includes a line he hasn't mentioned before. The voice said, in the King James, "it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks," like an ox kicking the goad that steers it. Paul had been fighting what was pulling him. He tells how he was sent to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light. Festus can't take it. He shouts: "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad." Paul answers calmly, I am not mad, most noble Festus. Then he turns to the king. King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do. And Agrippa replies with the line people still quote: "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." There's that word again from Antioch, Christian, in a king's mouth. What did Agrippa mean? Honestly, nobody's sure. The Greek is two short words, en oligo, in a little. It could mean almost, or in such a short time, or with so little effort. The Douay-Rheims reads it as in a little. He might be moved; he might be brushing Paul off with a smile. Paul's answer is beautiful either way: I would to God that not only you but all who hear me today were both almost, and altogether such as I am, "except these bonds." Picture him raising his chained hands. Then the king rises, and the hearing is over. Agrippa remarks this man could have gone free if he hadn't appealed to Caesar. So to Rome he goes.
screen: `HARD TO KICK AGAINST THE PRICKS.` · `THOU ART BESIDE THYSELF.` · `ALMOST THOU PERSUADEST ME.` · `EXCEPT THESE BONDS.` · then, large: `ALMOST, AND ALTOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't stop at almost. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've almost done for a long time. Almost called. Almost forgiven. Almost started. Almost gone to confession, or to Mass, or to the doctor. Whatever it is, name it quietly. Notice what has kept it at almost: fear, pride, the schedule, a little embarrassment. Now picture the next small step, just one, that would move it from almost to altogether. If you pray, you can offer that one step. The bell holds the time.
Almost. King Agrippa's answer to Paul, maybe moved, maybe joking, and Paul's wish that everyone be not almost but altogether. Today's word.
Your line: almost. Today, take one small, real step on something you've only almost done for too long. Day five hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics are encouraged to examine their consciences regularly, often at night, noticing what they have left undone as well as done, and many bring those things to the sacrament of reconciliation.

original.note: Greek: in a little. Agrippa's two words, which may mean almost, in so short a time, or with so little effort.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king nearly became a Christian.
what it means: Paul tells his story to a king, and the king's reply is so brief and slippery that nobody can say whether he was moved or mocking.
what a scholar hears: en oligō is ambiguous; the KJV says almost, the Douay in a little. this is also the second of only three times the word Christian appears in the New Testament.

notes: Confirm KJV wording of Acts 26:14, 26:24, 26:28 and 26:29.
Douay-Rheims 26:28 believed to read 'In a little thou persuadest me to become a Christian'; mentioned only as 'in a little', not quoted. Confirm.
'Two years in Caesarea' from Acts 24:27; confirm.
'Kick against the pricks' appears only in Acts 26:14 in critical texts (the KJV also has it at 9:5 from late manuscripts); the script says only that Paul hadn't mentioned it in his speech in Acts 22.
